newsitem.title: USA: USDA TRIMS 97/98 U.S. WHEAT IMPORT FORECAST.
newsitem.headline: USDA TRIMS 97/98 U.S. WHEAT IMPORT FORECAST.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department on Tuesday trimmed its forecast of 1997/98 U.S. wheat imports amid concerns over rising shipments from Canada.
In its monthly world Supply and Demand report, USDA pegged 1997/98 U.S. wheat, wheat flour and product imports at 2.59 million tonnes.
The new forecast is marginally higher than an estimated 2.51 million tonnes in 1996/97, but down nearly eight percent from USDA's July 1997/98 forecast of 2.72 million.
Virtually all U.S. wheat imports come from Canada.
In recent months, frictions linked to grain business between the two countries have risen after a few years of relative quiet.
In 1994-95, the U.S. imposed a one-year, 1.5-million-tonne quota on wheat imports from Canada. But since then, shipments have gradually edged up again.
In response to complaints from senators in the northern states, the U.S. Commerce Department is mulling whether to pursue anti-dumping action against Canada.
The senators have complained that the Canadian Wheat Board uses its monopoly control over Canadian wheat exports to unfairly undercut U.S. prices.
The lower U.S. wheat import forecast reflects revised outlooks for both the U.S. and Canadian wheat crop.
USDA raised its estimate of 1997/98 U.S. wheat production to 68.87 million tonnes, up more than 2.50 million.
At the same time, USDA cut its forecast of the 1997/98 Canadian crop to 23.50 million tonnes, down two million.
The higher U.S. forecast includes an improved outlook for the durum crop, most of which is grown in North Dakota.
Durum is used to make pasta.
USDA pegged the 1997/98 U.S. durum crop at 90.2 million bushels, up from last month's forecast of 80.1 million.
Based on the higher production, USDA lowered its forecast of 1997/98 durum imports to 25 million bushels, from 30 million last month.
The U.S. imported an estimated 23 million bushels of durum in 1996/97.
